title: GST/HST
summary: You sell → You collect the tax → You send it in → Done
subtitle: Collect it, track it, send it in, and claim back what you spent.

blocks.text: GST/HST is a sales tax you collect from customers on behalf of the government. The money is the government’s from the start, and handled well, it costs your business nothing. This lesson explains when you must register, how to claim back the tax you pay on business purchases, and when to file.
Know when to register, and get back every dollar of tax you are owed.
blocks.detail: Understanding the $30,000 limit and input tax credits keeps you out of trouble and puts money back in your pocket.
blocks.extra: Section 03 follows one sale from invoice to return.

blocks.text: When you register for GST/HST, the CRA gives you a GST/HST number and expects you to charge tax on most of your sales. You hold that tax for a short time, then send it in with a return. The rate is 5% GST in some provinces and a higher combined HST in others.

You are a small supplier if your taxable sales are $30,000 or less over four calendar quarters in a row, and in every single quarter. Small suppliers do not have to register. You can still sign up by choice, and many people do, because it lets you claim back the tax you pay on business costs.

If you pass the limit in a single quarter, you must charge tax on the sale that pushed you over and register within 29 days of that sale. If you pass it over four quarters instead, you stop being a small supplier at the end of the month after that quarter. Then you must start charging tax and register within 29 days.

Say you charge a client $2,000 for a service in a province with 5% GST. You add $100 of tax, so the client pays $2,100. Later you buy $300 of supplies and pay $15 of GST on them. You send the CRA the difference: $85.

The $15 you get back is called an input tax credit, or ITC. It recovers the GST/HST you pay on business purchases, and you claim it on your return. It applies only to the business share of a purchase, so a laptop you use half for personal things is only half claimable.

items.title: Charged on sales
items.text: Example: $100. What it is called: Tax collected.

items.title: Paid on purchases
items.text: Example: $15. What it is called: Input tax credit.

items.title: You send in
items.text: Example: $85. What it is called: Net tax.

blocks.text: You cannot claim personal purchases. The CRA does not allow input tax credits for things you buy for personal use or enjoyment. Keep personal and business purchases apart, and keep the proper receipt for each claim.

You have four years to claim. For most small businesses, an input tax credit must be claimed by the due date of the return for the last period ending within four years of the period you could first claim it. Don’t wait that long. Old receipts are the ones that go missing.

items.title: “Charging GST/HST means I lose money to the government.”
items.text: The tax belongs to the government from the moment you collect it. Your customer pays it, and you pass it along after taking off the credits you earned on your own purchases.

blocks.text: A simpler way: the Quick Method

The Quick Method lets you skip tracking most input tax credits. You still charge customers the full tax. But instead of working out the difference, you send in a fixed percentage of your sales, tax included. You also get a 1% credit on your first $30,000 of eligible sales each year.

You can use it if your taxable sales, including those of related businesses, were $400,000 or less. Some professions cannot use it, such as accountants, bookkeepers and lawyers. You can still claim credits on big purchases like computers and vehicles.

Check the Quick Method rate for your province. In Ontario, for example, the CRA’s guide gives 8.8% for service businesses on sales taxed at 13% HST. Your rate depends on your province and type of business, so look it up in CRA guide RC4058 before you sign up.
The Lens Cap
paragraphs: Teo Marchetti was a freelance photographer in Ottawa. He owned one lens cap, and he lost it every week. His goal was to buy a second lens for $2,600 so he could shoot weddings, which paid far more than portraits.

He was not registered for GST/HST, because his sales were nowhere near $30,000 in any quarter. Then a hotel offered him a corporate job worth $24,000, all paid in one quarter. He added it to his portrait work for those months. Thrilled and queasy, he saw the total would pass $30,000.

Teo faced a choice. He could stay quiet, charge the hotel no tax and hope nobody noticed. Or he could read the rule and do it right. He found the CRA page that afternoon. When one quarter goes over $30,000, you charge tax on the sale that pushed you over and register within 29 days. He added 13% HST to the quote and registered that week.

He worried the hotel would complain. Instead, the manager shrugged and said the hotel claimed the tax back anyway. Then came the twist. Now that Teo was registered, he could claim back the HST on his business purchases. The next month he bought the new lens and claimed the $338 of HST on it.

At his first filing, Teo sent in the difference and kept a tidy record of every receipt. The lens paid for part of itself. He still lost the lens cap every week, but his tax file was the one thing in his camera bag that never went missing.

blocks.text: Registering on time protects you, and the credits help pay your costs.
blocks.detail: A clear rule and a good record turn a scary moment into a routine one.
blocks.extra: Section 05 lists your filing dates and the steps to follow.

items.title: Track your sales by quarter.
items.text: Add up your taxable sales at the end of every calendar quarter and compare the total to $30,000.

items.title: Register when required, or earlier if it helps.
items.text: Signing up early lets you claim credits on business purchases.

items.title: Charge the right rate.
items.text: Charge the rate for where your customer is. Show the tax and your GST/HST number on every invoice.

items.title: Keep each receipt.
items.text: What the receipt shows decides your credit claim.

items.title: File and pay on time.
items.text: The dates depend on your reporting period, as shown below.

items.title: Monthly or quarterly
items.text: One month after the end of the reporting period

items.title: Annual, most businesses
items.text: Three months after your fiscal year-end

items.title: Sole proprietor, December 31 year-end, with business income
items.text: Pay by April 30 and file by June 15

blocks.text: Notes by province, and for your taxes

items.title: Instalments
items.text: An annual filer whose net tax for the last fiscal year was $3,000 or more may have to pay quarterly instalments.

items.title: Quebec
items.text: Quebec registrants deal with Revenu Québec for both GST and QST, so confirm the details with them.

items.title: Rates
items.text: GST is 5% in Alberta, B.C., Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Quebec and the territories. HST is 13% in Ontario, 14% in Nova Scotia and 15% in New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador and P.E.I. Rates change, so check the CRA’s rate page before you file.

items.title: “If I am a sole proprietor, my GST/HST is always due on June 15.”
items.text: That special date applies only to a person with business income and a December 31 year-end. Payment is still due April 30, so do not wait until June to pay.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Move the tax into a separate savings account the day each payment arrives. It was never yours, and a separate account keeps you from spending it by accident.
Quick Check

items.title: What is the small supplier limit?
items.detail: $30,000 over four calendar quarters in a row, and in any single quarter.

items.title: What is an input tax credit?
items.detail: A recovery of the GST/HST you paid on business purchases.

items.title: A sole proprietor with a December 31 year-end and business income files when?
items.detail: By June 15, with payment due April 30.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Your sales go over $30,000 in a single quarter. What must you do? A. Nothing until the end of the year · B. Charge the tax on the sale that pushed you over, and register within 29 days · C. Wait for the CRA to contact you
items.text: That is the rule for a single quarter. Waiting for the CRA is never the plan.

items.title: Which purchase can you claim an input tax credit on? A. A personal gift · B. Supplies used in your business · C. A family holiday
items.text: Credits apply only to the business part of your purchases and expenses.

items.title: Who can use the Quick Method? A. Any business with $400,000 or less in taxable sales, except certain professions · B. Only large companies · C. Only people who owe tax
items.text: Eligibility depends on your sales and your type of business.

items.title: In one sentence, say when you expect to register for GST/HST and why.
items.text: I will register when I get close to $30,000, or earlier if I buy equipment that I can claim credits on.

blocks.text: Track your sales every quarter, register on time, claim credits with proper receipts, and set the tax aside as you collect it.

items.title: GST/HST
items.text: A sales tax that registered businesses charge and send to the CRA.

items.title: Small supplier
items.text: A business with $30,000 or less in taxable sales over four quarters.

items.title: Input tax credit
items.text: A claim for the GST/HST you paid on business purchases.

items.title: Net tax
items.text: The tax you collected, minus your input tax credits.

items.title: Quick Method
items.text: A simpler way to work out the tax you send in.

items.title: Reporting period
items.text: The span of time one GST/HST return covers.
